title: A Tribute To The Far Side
summary: A tribute episode in the "Things We Love" series honoring the single-panel cartoon The Far Side by Gary Larson. The hosts cover Larson's upbringing in Tacoma, his biology-to-communications switch at Washington State, his early Nature's Way cartoons, the San Francisco Chronicle deal and syndication, the strip's growth and book success, its divisive reception, famous panels such as Early Experiments in Transportation, Midvale School for the Gifted, Cow Tools, and Lupus Slip-a-Phobia, his 1988 sabbatical and retirement, the final 1995 strip with Glinda the Goodwitch, the animated films, and his influence on scientists (a louse and a butterfly named after him, the thagamizer, and Jane Goodall cartoon controversy). The episode ends with a listener correction about dolphins being whales.
topics: final Far Side strip Wizard of Oz

segments.title: Opening and tribute series intro
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the Things We Love tribute episode on The Far Side and share why the cartoon shaped their humor.

segments.title: Single-panel cartoon versus comic strip
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why the single-panel cartoon is harder to pull off than a multi-panel strip, and how the strip's influence normalized its humor over time.

segments.title: Recurring archetypes and early life
segments.summary: The Far Side's stock characters are described, followed by Larson's birth in 1950, upbringing in Tacoma, family humor, and the influence of his older brother's love of nature.

segments.title: College, biology switch, and early jobs
segments.summary: Larson studied at Washington State, switched from biology to communications, and held jobs including banjo playing, a music store, and Humane Society investigator, where he created Nature's Way.

segments.title: Early sales and San Francisco Chronicle deal
segments.summary: Larson sold early cartoons, landed a Seattle Times gig, was dropped by that paper, then took his portfolio to the San Francisco Chronicle, which renamed the strip The Far Side and arranged syndication.

segments.title: Divisive reception
segments.summary: The hosts describe the strip's mixed reception, including a Buffalo newspaper rejection and editors who either loved or hated it.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Growth in papers and book success
segments.summary: The strip grew from thirty papers to a peak of about nineteen hundred, and Larson's books and calendars became bestsellers, with translations into seventeen languages.

segments.title: Awards and merchandising limits
segments.summary: Larson won cartoon awards and limited merchandising, refusing to take characters out of context, and was sensitive about how fans and critics perceived him.

segments.title: Offending people and the Far Side's philosophy
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the strip's recurring depictions of God and dogs versus cats, and a biographer's description of the strip as fools flailing against the universe.

segments.title: Famous panels: Early Experiments in Transportation
segments.summary: The hosts describe the cave-men wheel panel and how it leaves the ending to the viewer's imagination.

segments.title: Midvale School for the Gifted
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Midvale School for the Gifted panel, in which a kid pushes on a door marked pull.

segments.title: Cow Tools controversy
segments.summary: The 1982 Cow Tools panel confused readers, prompting Larson to write an explanatory letter; the hosts describe the panel as just bad cow-made tools.

segments.title: Lupus Slip-a-Phobia and Carrie Soper's pick
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Lupus Slip-a-Phobia panel, which Carrie Soper named as quintessential.

segments.title: Dog Threat Letter and Houdini regret
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Dog Threat Letter panel and Larson's regrets over it and the Harry Houdini panel.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Retirement pace and sabbatical
segments.summary: Larson drew seven strips a week, took a fourteen-month sabbatical in 1988 with his wife Tony Carmichael, then returned to five a week, citing fatigue and fear of mediocrity.

segments.title: Larson's shyness and the final strip
segments.summary: Larson disliked the spotlight, and the hosts describe the final Far Side strip from January 1995, with Glinda the Goodwitch and a Wizard of Oz ending.

segments.title: Animated films and children's books
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the 1994 to 1997 Tales from the Far Side films, a video game clip, Larson's 1999 children's book, and Mister Bear Squash You Flat.
topics: There's a Hair in My Dirt

segments.title: Science honors: species, thagamizer, and scientists
segments.summary: Scientists praised the strip, a louse and a butterfly were named for Larson, and the thagamizer term entered paleontology; E.O. Wilson and Stephen J. Gould wrote forewords.

segments.title: Jane Goodall cartoon controversy
segments.summary: A 1987 cartoon of apes prompted an angry letter from Sue Engel of the Jane Goodall Institute, but Goodall later found it funny and the cartoon was licensed by the institute.

segments.title: Larson today and website
segments.summary: The hosts note Larson is still alive, mention his website and occasional new work, and thank him.

segments.title: Listener correction on dolphins and whales
segments.summary: A listener named Josh corrects the hosts, noting that all dolphins are whales.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing credits and promotion for iHeartRadio podcasts.
